Rust's type system is strict and its inference is good. You write types where they document intent, and let inference handle the obvious cases.

Bindings

Immutable by default

This is not ceremony. Immutability by default means: when reading unfamiliar code you can assume most things do not change, and the compiler enforces it.

Shadowing vs mut

let x = 1; let x = x + 1; let mut x = 1; x += 1;
Type can change yes no
New memory location yes same
Usable inside closures while old value borrowed yes no
Value moved from the old binding possible n/a

Shadowing is idiomatic for transforming a value — parse a string, then re-bind as a number:

const vs static

Use const by default. Use static when you need a stable address or a non-Copy shared value (usually wrapped in OnceLock / LazyLock).

Primitive types

Category Types Notes
Signed ints i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 isize i32 is the default
Unsigned u8 u16 u32 u64 u128 usize u8 for bytes, usize for indices/lengths
Floats f32 f64 f64 default; no Eq, no Hash
Bool bool 1 byte
Char char 4 bytes, a Unicode scalar value — not a byte
String slice &str borrowed UTF-8, &'static str for literals
String String owned, growable UTF-8
Unit () the type of "no value"
Never ! type of panic!, return, loop {}

Numeric literals

Integer literals default to i32 unless context forces otherwise. This compiles because context supplies the type:

Conversions are explicit

Rust never implicitly converts between numeric types.

as truncates and wraps silently. When that matters, use the checked family:

Rule of thumb: use as only for widening (u32 as u64, f32 as f64) or when you have proven the range. Use try_from for narrowing.

Integer overflow

Build a + b overflowing
debug panics: "attempt to add with overflow"
release wraps silently

This is the classic "works on my machine" bug. If overflow is possible, be explicit: checked_*, saturating_*, wrapping_*.

Strings: &str vs String

The distinction trips up everyone. It is worth getting right early.

&str String
Ownership borrows owns
Growable no yes
Cost to pass pointer + length (16 bytes) move or borrow
Where it lives anywhere (stack, static, inside a String) heap

Rule of thumb: take &str in function parameters, return String when you must allocate.

Strings are UTF-8, so indexing is not allowed

s[0] is ambiguous: byte 0? char 0? They differ for any non-ASCII text. Use:

This is not a wart — it is the reason Rust programs do not mangle names in Kannada, Tamil, or any non-ASCII text.

Compound types

Arrays are fixed-length and stack-allocated. Vec<T> is the growable, heap-allocated version — module 02.06.

Type inference, and where it stops

Debug vs Display

Display must be implemented by hand because there is no correct default format for a user-facing message.

Mutability, precisely

Mutability is a property of the binding and of the borrow, and the compiler tracks both. That is module 02.03.

Exercises

  1. Write fn describe(n: i64) -> String that returns "zero", "negative" or "positive" — then try n: i128 and explain the change needed.
  2. Demonstrate overflow: a u8 counter incremented in a loop. Run it with cargo run and cargo run --release. Explain the two behaviours.
  3. Convert "300" to a u8 three ways: as, parse::<u8>(), and u8::try_from. Which succeed and which lose data?
  4. Write fn initials(full_name: &str) -> String that works correctly for "आदित्य शर्मा" and "Ada Lovelace". (Hint: chars(), not bytes.)
  5. Predict the type of let x = 0..10;. Check with let _: () = x; and read the compiler's error.
